---
title: "Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts"
---

[Part 3](03-collaborate.qmd) showed a conflict between two people sharing
`main`. This one is the version you will actually meet if your group follows
the pull-request discipline, and it looks different enough to be worth its own
walkthrough.

Everything below is real output from
[PR #2 of the example repository](https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic/pull/2).

## How you get here

Nobody did anything wrong. That is the point.

1. You branch off `main` and start writing.
2. While you are working, a teammate's pull request is merged. **`main` has
   moved on.**
3. Their change touched the same lines yours did.

Your branch is now based on a version of the project that no longer exists.

## Your push still works — and that is the trap

```bash
git push -u origin feature/limitations
```

``` text
 * [new branch]      feature/limitations -> feature/limitations
branch 'feature/limitations' set up to track 'origin/feature/limitations'
```

No rejection, no warning. **Branches never conflict on push**, because nobody
else is pushing to your branch. This is the opposite of Part 3, where the push
itself was rejected.

So you open the pull request happily:

```bash
gh pr create --base main --title "Note that the simulation guarantees correct specification"
```

``` text
https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic/pull/2
```

And *then* GitHub tells you.

## Finding out: ask, do not guess

On the PR page, the green merge button is replaced by a warning that the
branch has conflicts which must be resolved. From the terminal:

```bash
gh pr view 2 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus
```

``` text
PR #2  feature/limitations -> main
  mergeable        : CONFLICTING
  mergeStateStatus : DIRTY
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `UNKNOWN` just means "ask again in a moment"

GitHub works out mergeability in the background. Immediately after a push you
will often get:

``` text
mergeable: UNKNOWN   state: UNKNOWN
```

That is not a problem. Wait a few seconds and ask again.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> My pull request says it has conflicts. What conflicts, and what do I need to
> decide?
:::

## The fix: bring `main` into your branch

The direction matters, and it is the one thing to get right on this page.

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main       # main comes INTO your branch
```

``` text
Auto-merging report.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Why this direction and not the other

You could in principle merge your branch into `main` locally and push that.
**Do not.** It would put your unfinished, unreviewed work onto `main` directly,
bypassing the pull request and the teammate who was supposed to read it.

Resolve inside your own branch. `main` stays untouched until somebody merges
your PR. Your branch is your problem; `main` is the group's.
:::

## Reading this conflict: the sides are not equal

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    M1["main<br/>when you branched"] --> M2["main<br/>now"]
    M1 --> B1["your branch"]
    M2 -->|"git merge origin/main"| R["resolve<br/>here"]
    B1 --> R
    R -->|"git push"| PR["PR becomes<br/>MERGEABLE"]
```

The real conflict from PR #2:

``` text
<<<<<<< HEAD
This is a demonstration of the estimator on synthetic data. It is not
evidence about any real intervention.

A further limitation: the simulation assumes the arm effect is constant
across ages, so the model is correctly specified by construction. Real
data would not be so obliging.
=======
These data are synthetic. Nothing above is evidence about any real
intervention, and the numbers should not be quoted outside this course.
>>>>>>> origin/main
```

Now notice something that was not true in Part 3:

- `HEAD` is **your branch** — work nobody has reviewed yet
- below `=======` is **`main`** — work the group has *already accepted*

::: {.callout-important}
## Default to keeping `main`'s decision, and adding yours

In Part 3 both sides were equally provisional, so combining them was a
free choice. Here they are not. Somebody wrote that disclaimer, somebody else
reviewed it, and it was merged. Overwriting it with your own phrasing quietly
reverses a decision your group already made — and because it arrives inside a
conflict resolution, nobody will see it in review.

So the resolution kept `main`'s wording and *added* the separate point:

``` markdown
These data are synthetic. Nothing above is evidence about any real
intervention, and the numbers should not be quoted outside this course.

A further limitation: the simulation assumes the arm effect is constant
across ages, so the model is correctly specified by construction. Real
data would not be so obliging.
```

If you genuinely think `main` is wrong, that is a conversation in the pull
request, not a silent edit inside a merge.
:::

## The two checks, again

```bash
grep -nE '^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)' report.qmd || echo "clean"
quarto render report.qmd
```

``` text
clean
Output created: report.html
```

## Commit and push — to your branch

```bash
git add report.qmd
git commit -m "Merge main into feature/limitations"
git push
```

Plain `git push`, because you are still on your branch and it is already
tracking `origin`. You are **not** pushing to `main`.

Ask GitHub again:

```bash
gh pr view 2 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus
```

``` text
mergeable: MERGEABLE   state: CLEAN
```

The pull request updated itself. Your teammate can now review it and press
**Squash and merge**.

## The web "Resolve conflicts" button

GitHub offers to resolve simple conflicts in the browser. It works, and for a
one-line README clash it is fine.

::: {.callout-warning}
## But it cannot run your code

Resolving in the browser means you commit a file you have never rendered or
sourced. That is exactly how `<<<<<<< HEAD` reaches a submitted report, and
how a half-merged R script gets onto `main`.

For anything that has to execute — `.R`, `.qmd`, `.Rmd` — resolve locally and
render before you push.
:::

## Part 3 vs Part 3½, side by side

| | Part 3: shared `main` | Part 3½: pull request |
|---|---|---|
| Who collided | two people on `main` | your branch vs merged work |
| First symptom | **push rejected** | push succeeds; **PR says CONFLICTING** |
| Where you find out | terminal, immediately | GitHub, after you open the PR |
| Command that surfaces it | `git pull` | `git merge origin/main` |
| Sides in the conflict | two drafts, equal standing | your draft vs **accepted** work |
| Default resolution | combine both | keep `main`, add yours |
| What you push afterwards | `main` | your branch |

Same mechanism underneath: two changes to the same lines, and a human decides.
Only the moment of discovery differs.
